hook: On a shaded map of South Asia by total population, India is the darkest country and Bangladesh is a class lighter. A quick reader decides India is the most crowded place in the region. It is not: Bangladesh fits far more people on each square kilometer (UN World Population Prospects 2024). The map was right. The reading was wrong, because the reader skipped the legend.

figure.caption: Read the title, then the legend and units, then the source line, and only then describe the pattern.

chain.effect: you know whether a shade or a number is a total, a percent or a rate per 1,000 people

ideas: A legend (or key) says what each shade, symbol or line on a map stands for. Read it before you look at the colors.
Check the units. A total (number of people) favors big places; a percent or a rate (per 1,000 people) lets you compare places of any size.
A source line names who made the data and the year. "Invented data for practice" means the numbers are made up for the exercise.
A trend is a change over time. Describe it with its direction, its dates and how much it changed.

misconception.wrong: The darkest country on a shaded map has the "most" of everything, so it is the most crowded or the most important.
misconception.right: The darkest country has the most of whatever the legend measures. If the legend counts totals, a big country like India is dark simply because it is big.

summary: Read every map, table and chart in the same order: title, legend and units, source line, then the pattern. The units tell you whether you are looking at a total, a percent or a rate, which changes what you can claim. A strong pattern statement names real places and gives values, and a trend gives its direction, dates and size.
